label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $B=\mathcal{A}\oplus N$ be a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. The operation \eqref{eq:circdef} is well-defined and commutative on $B^{++}$. Moreover, $(B^{++},\circ)$ is a semigroup if and only if $[[x,y],z]=0$ holds for all $x,y,z\in B$.
head: environment

label: def_split
title: Definition
head: environment

label: remsplit
title: Remark
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
{\ }
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Every $C^*$-algebra $\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}}$ can be seen as a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra $\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}}=\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}} \oplus 0$.
\item Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a commutative $C^*$-algebra and let $N_0$ be a nilpotent $\mathbb{C}$-algebra. Define $N_1=\mathbb{C}\cdot 1 \oplus N_0$ and $B=\mathcal{A} \otimes_\mathbb{C} N_1$. Then $\mathcal{A}\otimes_\mathbb{C} 1$ is a subalgebra isomorphic to~$\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{A}\otimes_\mathbb{C} N_0$ is nilpotent, their elements commute and their direct sum is isomorphic to~$B$. 
\item Consider the subalgebra $B_3$ of $\operatorname{M}_3(\mathbb C)$ defined by
\[
B_3=
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
a & c_1 & c_2 \\
0 & a & c_3 \\
0 & 0 & a
\end{pmatrix}
\; \Bigg\vert \; a,c_1,c_2,c_3\in \mathbb C
\right\}.
\]
Then $B_3$ is a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. Indeed, set $\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{C} I_3$ and
\[
N=
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & c_1 & c_2\\
0 & 0 & c_3\\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\; \Bigg\vert \; c_1,c_2,c_3\in \mathbb C
\right\}.
\]
Then, $\mathcal{A}$ is a unital subalgebra of $B_3$, which is a $C^*$-algebra isomorphic to
$\mathbb{C}$, and $1_{\mathcal{A}}=I_3=1_{B_3}$. Moreover, $N$ is an ideal of $B_3$ which consists of nilpotent elements. More precisely, $N^3=0$. Finally, every element of $B_3$ can be written uniquely as
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
a & c_1 & c_2\\
0 & a & c_3\\
0 & 0 & a
\end{pmatrix}
=
aI_3+
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & c_1 & c_2\\
0 & 0 & c_3\\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
so that $B_3=\mathcal{A} \oplus N$. Since $\mathcal A$ consists of scalar matrices, every element of $\mathcal A$ commutes with every element of $N$. Therefore, $B_3$ satisfies all the conditions in~\Cref{def_split}.
\end{enumerate}

title: Example
head: environment

label: rem_square
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{rem_square}
Let $B=\mathcal{A}\oplus N$ be a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. 
For any $x=a+n \in B^{++}$ there exists a unique square root of $x$ in
$B^{++}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x=a+n\in B^{++}$ and let $b=\sqrt a$. Since $a\in \mathcal{A}^{++}$,
we have $b\in \mathcal{A}^{++}$ and $b$ is invertible. Moreover, since
$n$ is nilpotent, there exists $k\in\mathbb N$ such that $n^k=0$. Since
the elements of $\mathcal{A}$ and $N$ commute, we also have
\[
(b^{-2}n)^k=0.
\]
Thus, the series
\[
(1+t)^{1/2}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \binom{1/2}{j} t^j,
\]
where
\[
\binom{1/2}{0}=1 \quad \text{ and } \quad
\binom{1/2}{j}=\frac{\left(\frac12\right)\left(\frac12-1\right)\cdots\left(\frac12-j+1\right)}{j!},\quad \text{for any } j\geq 1,
\]
becomes a finite sum when evaluated at $t=b^{-2}n$. We may therefore define
\[
y=b\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\binom{1/2}{j}(b^{-2}n)^j .
\]
Then $y\in B^{++}$, and since $b$ commutes with $n$, we get
\[
y^2=b^2
\left(
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\binom{1/2}{j}(b^{-2}n)^j
\right)^2
=b^2(1+b^{-2}n)=a+n=x.
\]
Hence $y$ is a square root of $x$ in $B^{++}$. The uniqueness of $y$ follows from the uniqueness of the positive square root in the quotient $B/N\cong \mathcal{A}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $B=\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}} \oplus N$ and $B'=\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}}' \oplus N'$ be split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebras. A \emph{morphism} $B \to B'$ is a morphism of associative algebra split extensions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
N \arrow [r, "i"] \ar[d, "f"']
&B \arrow[r, shift left, "\pi_1"] \ar[d, swap, "g"]&
\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}} \ar[l, shift left, "j"] \ar[d, "h"] \\
N' \arrow [r, "i'"]
&B' \arrow[r, shift left, "\pi'"] &
\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}}' \ar[l, shift left, "j'"] 
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
such that $h$ is a unital $^*$-homomorphism. In other words, $f$, $g$, and $h$ are homomorphisms of associative algebras, $h$ is moreover a unital $^*$-homomorphism, and the following identities hold:
\[
g\circ i=i'\circ f,\qquad
h\circ \pi_1=\pi'_1\circ g,\qquad
g\circ j=j'\circ h.
\]

label: lm:seminorm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:seminorm}
Let $B=\mathcal{A}\oplus N$ be a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. Let $u(\tau)\in \mathbb{C}[[\tau]]$ be a formal power series and assume that $u(\tau)$ has convergence radius $\rho >0$ at $0$. If $x,y\in B$, $\|x\|_s<\rho$, and $xy=yx$, then $u(x)$ and $y$ commute.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $x=a+n, y=a'+n' \in B$. If $(a+n)(a'+n')=(a'+n')(a+n)$, then $aa'=a'a$ and $nn'=n'n$. Hence, $a'$ and $n'$ commute with $u^{(i)}(a)$ and $n^i$ for any $0 \leq i \leq M-1$ respectively, which implies that $u(a+n)$ and $a'+n'$ commute, since $\|x\|_s < \rho$.
head: environment

label: lm:sqrt
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:sqrt}
Let $B=\mathcal{A}\oplus N$ be a split $ C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra and let $s(\xi)$ be the formal power series as in \eqref{eq:formalsroot}. The following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $x\in B$ with $\|x\|_s<1$, then $\|1-s(x)\|_s\leq 1-\sqrt{1-\|x\|_s}$.
\item If $x,y\in B$ with $\|x\|_s < 1$ and $\|1-y\|_s<1$, then $y^2=1+x$ holds if and only if $y=s(x)$.
\item There exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that, for each pair of commuting elements $x,y\in B$ with $\|x\|_s < \varepsilon$ and $\|y\|_s < \varepsilon$, one has $s(x)s(y)=s(x+y+xy)$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Let $x\in B$ with $\|x\|_s<1$. Thus
\begin{align*}
\|1-s(x)\|_s &= \left\|{\frac {1}{2}}(-x)+{\frac {1}{8}}{(-x)}^{2}+{\frac {1}{16}}{(-x)}^{3}+{\frac {5}{128}}{(-x)}^{4}+\cdots\right\|_s \\
&\leq {\frac {1}{2}}\|-x\|_s+{\frac {1}{8}}{\|-x\|_s}^{2}+{\frac {1}{16}}{\|-x\|_s}^{3}+{\frac {5}{128}}{\|-x\|_s}^{4}+\cdots \\
&= 1-s(-\|-x\|_s) \\
&= 1-\sqrt{1-\|x\|_s}.
\end{align*}
\item Let $y\in {B}$ such that $\|1-y\|_s<1$. If $y=s(x)$, then trivially $y^2=1+x$. Conversely, if $y^2=1+x$, then 
\[
\|1-s(x)\|_s\leq 1-\sqrt{1-\|x\|_s}<1,
\]
and
\[
\|2-s(x)-y\|_s \leq \|1-s(x)\|_s+\|1-y\|_s<2,
\]
which implies $\|1-\frac{s(x)+y}{2}\|_s<1$. Hence, $s(x)+y$ is invertible in ${B}$. As $y$ commutes with $x=y^2-1$, and $y$ commutes with $s(x)$ by \Cref{lm:seminorm}, then $y^2=s(x)^2$ implies $0=(y-s(x))(y+s(x))$. Since the second factor is invertible, we have $y-s(x)=0$. 
\item We can choose $\varepsilon>0$ \footnote{This is always true for $\varepsilon < \sqrt{2}-1$.} such that $\|x+y+xy\|_s<1$ and $\|1-s(x)s(y)\|_s<1$, for any $\|x\|_s < \varepsilon$ and $\|y\|_s<\varepsilon$. By \Cref{lm:seminorm}, $z_1=s(x)$, $z_2=s(y)$ and $z_3=s(x+y+xy)$ commute since $xy=yx$. We saw that $z_1^2=1+x$, $z_2^2=1+y$ and 
\[
z_3^2=1+x+y+xy=(1+x)(1+y)=z_1^2z_2^2=(z_1z_2)^2.
\]
Thus, $z_3=z_1z_2$ follows from (ii).  
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: lm:sqrtB+
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:sqrtB+}
Let $B=\mathcal{A}\oplus N$ be a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. For any $a\in \mathcal{A}$ and $n\in N$, the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $n\in N$, then $s(n)\in 1+N$ and $s(n)^2=1+n$.
\item The map $n\mapsto s(n)$ is a bijection from $N$ to $1+N$. In particular, any element $y\in 1+N$ has a unique square root $\sqrt{y}=s(y-1) \in 1+N$.
\item Every element of $B^{++}$ has a unique square root in $B^{++}$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item It is an immediate consequence of \Cref{rem_square}.
\item For any $n\in N$, $s(n^2+2n)=s(n)^2=1+n$ by (iii) of \Cref{lm:sqrt} with $x=y=n$. Hence, for $y\in 1+N$, we have $s(y^2-1)=y$, which means that the map $x\mapsto s(x)$ is surjective. The injectivity follows from
\[
s(n_1)=s(n_2) \Rightarrow 1+n_1=s(n_1)^2=s(n_2)^2=1+n_2 \Rightarrow n_1=n_2.
\]
\item Fix an element $a+n\in B^{++}$. As $a$, $\sqrt{a}$ and $n$ commute, and $a^{-1}n\in N$, we have
\[
(\sqrt{a}\, s(a^{-1}n))^2 = a\, s(a^{-1}n)^2 =a(1+a^{-1}n)=a+n.
\]
The uniqueness follows from the uniqueness of the square root in $\mathcal{A}^{++}$ and in $1+N$. 
\end{enumerate}

The operations \eqref{eq:circdef}, \eqref{eq:sharpdef} and \eqref{eq:stardef} are well-defined on $B^{++}$. Furthermore, the operation \eqref{eq:circdef} is commutative on $B^{++}$.

label: lm:jacobi
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:jacobi}
Let $A$ be an associative algebra over the field $\mathbb{F}$, with $\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{F})\neq 2,3$. Let $S$ be a vector subspace of $A$ that is closed under the ternary Lie bracket $[[-,-],-]$. Assume that $[[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]=0$, for any $x,y\in S$. Then $[[x,y],z]=0$, for any $x,y,z\in S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Linearizing $[[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]=0$ in $y$, since $\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{F})\neq 2$, we get $[[x,y],z]+[[x,z],y]=0$ for any $x,y,z\in S$. Hence
\[
[[x,y],z]=[[z,x],y]=[[y,z],x].
\]
We substitute this in the Jacobi identity
\[
[[x,y],z]+[[y,z],x]+[[z,x],y]=0
\]
to obtain $3[[x,y],z]=0$, for any $x,y,z\in S$. Thus, $[[x,y],z]=0$ holds in $S$.
head: environment

label: lm:lts
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:lts}
Let $B=\mathcal{A}\oplus N$ be a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. Assume that for some $\varepsilon>0$, the identity $[[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]=0$ holds for any $x,y\in B^{++}$ such that $\|x\|_s< \varepsilon$, $\|y\|_s<\varepsilon$. Then $[[x,y],z]=0$, for any $x,y,z \in B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We denote
\[
\Sigma = \{a+n\in B \mid \text{$a$ is self-adjoint}\}
\]
and we fix arbitrary elements $x,y\in \Sigma$. Then there exist real numbers $\alpha,\beta > 0$ such that 
\[
x'=\alpha x+\beta\cdot 1, \quad y'=\alpha y+\beta\cdot 1\in B^{++}
\]
and $\|x'\|_s< \varepsilon$, $\|y'\|_s<\varepsilon$. By assumption and the properties of the Lie bracket, we have
\[
0=[[x',y'],y']-[[y',x'],x']=\alpha^3([[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]).
\]
As $\Sigma$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-vector space, \Cref{lm:jacobi} implies that $[[x,y],z]=0$, for any $x,y,z\in \Sigma$. It is well known that any element of a $C^*$-algebra can be written as $a+ib$ with $a,b$ self-adjoint. In this way, any element of $B$ can be written as $x+iy$, with $x,y\in \Sigma$. This implies that $[[x,y],z]=0$, for any $x,y,z\in B$.
head: environment

title: Remark
head: environment

label: pr:lts
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pr:lts}
Let $B=\mathcal{A}\oplus N$ be a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. If the identity $[[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]=0$ holds in $B^{++}$, then
\[
x\circ y = (\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})^2,
\]
for any $x,y \in B^{++}$.

label: cor_if
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor_if}
If the identity $[[x,y],z]=0$ holds in $B$, then $(B^{++},\circ)$ is a semigroup. \hfil\qed
head: environment

label: pr:Cstar_lts
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pr:Cstar_lts}
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a $C^*$-algebra such that $[[x,y],y]=0$ for any $x,y \in \mathcal{A}^{++}$. Then $\mathcal{A}$ is commutative.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By the Kleinecke-Shirokov Theorem (see~\cite{MR0087914} and~\cite{Shi56}), $[[x,y],y]=0$ implies that $[x,y]$ is quasi-nilpotent, and thus, $\operatorname{spec}({[x,y]})=\{0\}$. If $x,y \in \mathcal{A}^{++}$, then $i[x,y]$ is self-adjoint, and $\|[x,y]\|=\|i[x,y]\|$ is equal to the spectral radius. This means that $[x,y]=0$ holds in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}}^{++}$. Finally, if all positive elements commute, then all self-adjoint elements do so, and thus, we obtain the commutativity of $\mathcal{A}$.
head: environment

label: lm:prodrule
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:cxody
title: Proof
body_md:
We can choose $\varepsilon >0$ small enough\footnote{It is enough to choose again $\varepsilon < \sqrt{3-2\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}-1$.} such that, if $\|x-1\|_s,\|y-1\|_s<\varepsilon$ then
\[
\|x(x^{-1}\# y)-1\|_s, \|(x^{-1}\# y)x-1\|_s, \|xy-1\|_s, \|yx-1\|_s < 1.
\]
If $x,y\in B^{++}$, then by (ii) of \Cref{lm:sqrt} and equation \eqref{8++}, we have
\[
x(x^{-1}\# y)=s(xy-1), \qquad (x^{-1}\# y)x=s(yx-1).
\]
In other words, if $x,y\in B$ are such that $\|x\|_s,\|y\|_s<\varepsilon$, then $1+x,1+y\in B^{++}$, and
\begin{align*}
(1+x)((1+x)^{-1}\# (1+y)) &= s(x+y+xy),\\
((1+x)^{-1}\# (1+y))(1+x) &= s(x+y+yx).
\end{align*}
We take now $c,d>0$ and $\|x\|_s<c\varepsilon$, $\|y\|_s<d\varepsilon$. Then
\begin{align*}
(c+x)((c+x)^{-1}\# (d+y)) &= \sqrt{cd} \, s\left(\frac{x}{c} + \frac{y}{d} + \frac{xy}{cd}\right),\\
((c+x)^{-1}\# (d+y))(c+x) &= \sqrt{cd} \, s\left(\frac{x}{c} + \frac{y}{d} + \frac{yx}{cd}\right).
\end{align*}
By equation \eqref{eq:circbysharp}, one has
\begin{align*} \label{eq:cxody}
(c+x)\circ (d+y) &= c+d+x+y+\sqrt{cd} \left(s\left(\frac{x}{c} + \frac{y}{d} + \frac{xy}{cd}\right) + s\left(\frac{x}{c} + \frac{y}{d} + \frac{yx}{cd}\right)
\right) \\
&= c+d+x+y+\sqrt{cd} \left(\hat{s}\left(\frac{x}{c},\frac{y}{d}\right) +2 +\frac{x}{c} + \frac{y}{d} \right) \\
&= (\sqrt{c}+\sqrt{d})^2+(\sqrt{c}+\sqrt{d})\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{c}}+\frac{y}{\sqrt{d}}\right) + \sqrt{cd} \, \hat{s}\left(\frac{x}{c},\frac{y}{d}\right).
\end{align*}
This proves \eqref{eq:prodrule}. Furthermore
\begin{align*}
\|(c+x)\circ (d+y) - (\sqrt{c}+\sqrt{d})^2\|_s &= \|x+y+\sqrt{cd} \left(s\left(\alpha \right)+s\left(\beta\right)-2\right)\|_s \\
&\leq \|x\|_s + \|y\|_s + \sqrt{cd}(\|\alpha\|_s + \|\beta \|_s) \\
&< \varepsilon c + \varepsilon d + (4\varepsilon + 2\varepsilon^2)\sqrt{cd} \\
&< 3(\sqrt{c}+\sqrt{d})^2\varepsilon,
\end{align*}
where $\alpha=\dfrac{x}{c}+\dfrac{y}{d}+\dfrac{xy}{cd}$ and $\beta=\dfrac{x}{c}+\dfrac{y}{d}+\dfrac{yx}{cd}$. Thus, \eqref{eq_lemma5.1} holds.

label: lm:shatlow
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:s_sym_terms
title: Proof
head: environment

label: pr:Axy_expansion
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:Bxy
title: Proof
body_md:
We define
\[
B(x,y) = ((1+x) \circ 1) \circ (1+y).
\]
As $1+x,1+y \in B^{++}$ and $(1+x) \circ (1 \circ (1+y)) = ((1+y) \circ 1) \circ (1+x) = B(y,x)$ for the commutativity of \eqref{eq:circdef}, we have
\[
A(x,y)=B(x,y)-B(y,x).
\]
We choose $\varepsilon>0$ such that \Cref{lm:prodrule} holds for $\varepsilon'=3\varepsilon$ and we define $w$ by
\[
(1+x)\circ 1 = 4 +2x +\hat{s}(x,0) = 4+w.
\]
By \eqref{eq_lemma5.1}, $\|w\|_s<12\varepsilon=4\varepsilon'$ and we can apply again \Cref{lm:prodrule} with $1+y$ and $4+w$. Thus, by \eqref{eq:prodrule} we obtain
\begin{align*}
B(x,y) &= (4+w)\circ (1+y) \\
&= 9+3\left(\frac{w}{2}+y\right) +2\hat{s}\left(\frac{w}{4},y\right) \\
&= 9+3(x+y) + \frac{3}{2}\hat{s}(x,0) + 2\hat{s}\left(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\hat{s}(x,0),y\right). 
\end{align*}
By \Cref{lm:shatlow}, we have that the low degree terms of $B(x,y)$ are given by
\begin{multline*} \label{eq:Bxy}
B(x,y)=9+3(x+y)-\frac{1}{4}(2x^2-xy-yx+2y^2)+ \\ 
\frac{1}{32}(8x^3-x^2y-2xyx-yx^2-4yxy+8y^3) + O(4).
\end{multline*}  
As the conditions for $x$ and $y$ were the same, we can interchange them to obtain
\begin{align*}
A(x,y)& = \frac{1}{32}(xy^2-2yxy+y^2x-x^2y+2xyx-yx^2)+O(4)\\
&=\dfrac{1}{32}([[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]) + O(4). \qedhere
\end{align*}
head: environment

label: prop17
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop17}
Let $B=\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}} \oplus N$ be a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. If $(B^{++}, \circ)$ is a semigroup, then $[[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]=0$ for every $x,y \in B^{++}$ with $\|x\|_s<\varepsilon$ and $\|y\|_s<\varepsilon$, for some $\varepsilon > 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that the operation \eqref{eq:circdef} is associative on $B^{++}$. It is sufficient to show that $[[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]=0$
holds whenever $x,y\in N$, or $x,y\in \mathcal{A}^{++}$ with $\|x\|<\varepsilon$ and $\|y\|<\varepsilon$, for some $\varepsilon>0$. As the elements of $\mathcal{A}$ and $N$ commute, this implies $[[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x]=0$, for every $x,y\in B^{++}$ with $\|x\|_s<\varepsilon$ and $\|y\|_s<\varepsilon$.

Let us choose $\varepsilon>0$ according to \Cref{lm:prodrule} and fix the elements $x,y\in B^{++}$ such that $\|x\|_s< \varepsilon$ and $\|y\|_s<\varepsilon$. If $\varepsilon'=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{\max\lbrace \|x\|_s,\|y\|_s\rbrace}$, then by \Cref{pr:Axy_expansion}, for any $0<t<\varepsilon'$ we have that $\|tx\|_s < \varepsilon$, $\|ty\|_s < \varepsilon$, and
\begin{equation}
0=A(tx,ty)=\sum_{i=3}^{\infty} z_i t^{i},
\end{equation}
where $z_3=\dfrac{1}{32}([[x,y],y]-[[y,x],x])$, and $z_i$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree~$i$ in the non-commuting variables $x,y$.

We prove the proposition by showing $z_3=0$. Let us first assume that $z_3\neq 0$ and $x,y\in N$. Let $k$ be the least positive integer such that $z_3\in N^k\setminus N^{k+1}$. For infinitely many choices of $t$, we have 
\begin{equation*}
z_3+z_4t+\cdots + z_{k} t^{k-3} \in N^{k+1},
\end{equation*}
which implies $z_3, z_4, \ldots, z_k \in N^{k+1}$, a contradiction.

Now, let $x,y\in \mathcal{A}^{++}$. Then $\|x\|< \varepsilon$, $\|y\|<\varepsilon$, the series 
\[
\sum_{i=4}^{\infty} z_i t^{i-3}
\]
is absolutely convergent and it tends to $0$ if $t\to 0$. Hence, we conclude that 
\[
z_3=-\sum_{i=4}^{\infty} z_i t^{i-3}=0.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $B=\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}} \oplus N$ be a split $C^*$-by-nilpotent algebra. By \Cref{pr:B_oper_welldef}, we have that the operation \eqref{eq:circdef} is well-defined and commutative on $B^{++}$.

Furthermore, if we suppose that $(B^{++}, \circ)$ is a semigroup, then by \Cref{prop17} and \Cref{lm:lts} the identity $[[x,y],z]=0$ holds in $B$.

Conversely, if $[[x,y],z]=0$ for any $x,y,z \in B$, then by \Cref{cor_if} we have that $x \circ y=(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})^2$, and \eqref{eq:circdef} is associative on $B^{++}$.
head: environment
